opts: is concave upward for all values of $t\in(-\infty,\infty)$.
is concave downward for all values of $t\in(0,\infty)$.
is concave upward only for $t>0$ and concave downward for $t<0$.
hints: Concavity of a parametric curve is decided by the sign of the second derivative $d^2y/dx^2$.
Find $dy/dx$ as $\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$, then differentiate with respect to $t$ and divide by $dx/dt$ again.

For $x=x(t)$, $y=y(t)$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}$ and $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{x'(t)}$; concave up where this is positive, and the tangent is horizontal where $y'(t)=0$.
steps: $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}(2t)}{1}=2>0$ for every $t$, so the curve is concave upward for all $t$.
Check the others: the slope $2t$ equals $-2$ at $t=-1$ (not $2$), and equals $2\neq0$ at $t=1$, so there is no horizontal tangent there.

qs.q: The graph of the parametric curve \[ x=\frac{4}{\cos t},\quad y=\frac{3\sin t}{\cos t} \] is
hints: Eliminate the parameter and recognise the resulting conic.
Rewrite $x$ and $y$ using $\sec t$ and $\tan t$, then isolate those two functions.
Use the identity $1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t$, equivalently $\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t=1$; an equation $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is a hyperbola.
steps: Write $x=4\sec t$ and $y=3\tan t$, so $\sec t=\dfrac x4$ and $\tan t=\dfrac y3$.
This is the standard form of a hyperbola.

qs.q: The vector component of $\vec u=\langle -9,-2,-4\rangle$ orthogonal to $\vec v=\langle 0,4,4\rangle$ is
hints: Split $\vec u$ into a part parallel to $\vec v$ and a part orthogonal to $\vec v$.
First compute the projection of $\vec u$ onto $\vec v$ using a dot product, then subtract it from $\vec u$.
$\operatorname{proj}_{\vec v}\vec u=\dfrac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{\|\vec v\|^2}\vec v$, and the orthogonal component is $\vec u-\operatorname{proj}_{\vec v}\vec u$.
steps: The orthogonal component is $\vec u-\left(-\dfrac34\vec v\right)=\vec u+\dfrac34\vec v$.
qs.brief: $\mathrm{proj}=\frac{-24}{32}\vec v=-\frac34\vec v$, so the orthogonal part is $\vec u+\frac34\vec v$.

qs.q: If the area of the surface generated by revolving the parametric curve \[ x=\frac{t^3}{3},\quad y=t+1,\quad 1\le t\le 2, \] about the $y$-axis, is equal to $\dfrac{\pi}{9}\left(a^{3/2}-b^{3/2}\right)$, then $a+b=$
hints: This is the surface area of a solid of revolution for a parametric curve.
Revolving about the $y$-axis uses the distance $x$ from the axis as the radius; set up the integral in $t$ and look for a substitution.
For revolution about the $y$-axis: $S=2\pi\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x(t)\sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^2+\left(y'(t)\right)^2}\,dt$.

qs.q: The slope of the tangent line to the polar curve \[ r=2(1-\cos\theta) \] at the point corresponding to $\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ is equal to
hints: Treat the polar curve as a parametric curve with parameter $\theta$.
Write $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$, differentiate both with respect to $\theta$ and take the ratio at the given angle.
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\sin\theta+r\cos\theta}{\frac{dr}{d\theta}\cos\theta-r\sin\theta}$.

qs.q: The polar equation $r^2=4\sec\theta\csc\theta$ can be converted to the rectangular equation
hints: Convert using $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$.
Rewrite the right side with $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$ in the denominator and clear them by multiplying.
$x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, so $xy=r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

opts: a limacon with an inner loop
hints: Convert the equation to polar coordinates and compare with the standard polar curves.
Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ and simplify, using a double-angle identity.
$x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$; curves $r=a\sin n\theta$ with $n$ even are roses with $2n$ petals.
steps: Hence $r=\pm\sin 2\theta$, which is the same curve as $r=\sin2\theta$.

qs.q: The area of the region enclosed by the cardioid $r=2(1+\cos\theta)$ is equal to
hints: Use the area formula in polar coordinates.
Square $r$, expand, and use a half-angle identity for $\cos^2\theta$; integrate over a full turn.
$A=\dfrac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,d\theta$ and $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$.
steps: Over $[0,2\pi]$ the cosine terms integrate to $0$, leaving $2\cdot\dfrac32\cdot2\pi=6\pi$.

qs.q: The product of all possible values of $\alpha$ such that the points \[ P(0,2,1),\ Q(\alpha-1,0,\alpha),\ R(5,-\alpha,6) \] are collinear, is equal to
hints: Three points are collinear when the vectors joining them are parallel.
Form $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}$ and require one to be a scalar multiple of the other (or their cross product to be zero).
$\vec a\parallel\vec b$ exactly when $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec 0$, i.e. corresponding components are proportional; for a quadratic $\alpha^2+p\alpha+q=0$ the product of the roots is $q$.
steps: Parallel: the first and third components give the same ratio, so we need $\dfrac{\alpha-1}{5}=\dfrac{-2}{-\alpha-2}$.

qs.q: Let $\alpha$ be the angle between the two nonzero vectors $\vec u$ and $\vec v$. If \[ \vec u\cdot\vec v=-1\quad\text{and}\quad \|\vec u\times\vec v\|=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}, \] then $\sec(\alpha)=$
hints: The dot product carries $\cos\alpha$ and the cross product magnitude carries $\sin\alpha$, with the same factor $\|\vec u\|\|\vec v\|$.
Divide the cross product magnitude by the dot product to cancel the lengths and get $\tan\alpha$, then use the sign of the dot product to locate $\alpha$.
$\vec u\cdot\vec v=\|\vec u\|\|\vec v\|\cos\alpha$, $\|\vec u\times\vec v\|=\|\vec u\|\|\vec v\|\sin\alpha$ with $0\le\alpha\le\pi$, and $\sec\alpha=\pm\sqrt{1+\tan^2\alpha}$.
steps: The dot product is negative, so $\cos\alpha<0$ and $\alpha$ is obtuse: $\alpha=150^\circ$.

qs.q: The area of the region inside the circle $r=1$ and outside of the cardioid $r=1-\cos\theta$ is equal to
hints: This is the area between two polar curves; find where they meet first.
Set the two radii equal to get the limits, use symmetry about the $x$-axis, and subtract the squared inner radius from the squared outer radius.
$A=\dfrac12\int_\alpha^\beta\left(r_{\text{outer}}^2-r_{\text{inner}}^2\right)d\theta$, and $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}$.
steps: For $-\dfrac\pi2\le\theta\le\dfrac\pi2$ we have $1-\cos\theta\le1$, so the circle is outer there. By symmetry $A=2\cdot\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(1-(1-\cos\theta)^2\right)d\theta$.

qs.q: If the standard equation of the sphere with center $(-4,5,6)$ and tangent to the $yz$-plane is $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2=r^2$, then $a+b+c+r^2=$
hints: Tangent to a coordinate plane means the radius equals the distance from the center to that plane.
Decide which coordinate of the center gives the distance to the $yz$-plane, then read off $a,b,c$ from the center.
The $yz$-plane is $x=0$, so the distance from $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ to it is $|x_0|$; the sphere with center $(a,b,c)$ is $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2=r^2$.
steps: The distance from the center to the plane $x=0$ is $|-4|=4$, so $r=4$ and $r^2=16$.

qs.q: The triangle with the vertices \[ P(1,2,0),\ Q(0,0,0),\ R(-2,1,0) \]
hints: Test the angles using dot products of the side vectors, and the area using a cross product.
Form the side vectors from each vertex and compute their dot products to look for a zero.
Two vectors are perpendicular iff $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$; the area of a triangle with sides $\vec a,\vec b$ from one vertex is $\dfrac12\|\vec a\times\vec b\|$.
steps: So the angle at $Q$ is $90^\circ$ and the triangle is a right triangle.
Area check: $\dfrac12\|\overrightarrow{QP}\times\overrightarrow{QR}\|=\dfrac12\cdot5=\dfrac52$, which is neither $5$ nor $10$.

qs.q: The value of $c$ for which the three vectors \[ \vec u=\langle1,c,-7\rangle,\quad \vec v=\langle2,-1,c\rangle,\quad \vec w=\langle0,-9,18\rangle \] are coplanar (lie in the same plane) is
hints: Three vectors are coplanar when the parallelepiped they span is flat, i.e. has zero volume.
Set the scalar triple product, a $3\times3$ determinant of the components, equal to zero and solve for $c$.
$\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are coplanar iff $\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)=\det\begin{bmatrix}u_1&u_2&u_3\\v_1&v_2&v_3\\w_1&w_2&w_3\end{bmatrix}=0$.

qs.q: If the angle between the two unit vectors $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ is $120^\circ$, then $\|\vec B-\vec A\|=$
hints: Compute the square of the length using the dot product.
Expand $\|\vec B-\vec A\|^2=(\vec B-\vec A)\cdot(\vec B-\vec A)$ and use the angle to get $\vec A\cdot\vec B$.
$\|\vec v\|^2=\vec v\cdot\vec v$ and $\vec A\cdot\vec B=\|\vec A\|\|\vec B\|\cos\theta$.
steps: $\|\vec B-\vec A\|^2=\|\vec B\|^2-2\vec A\cdot\vec B+\|\vec A\|^2=1+1+1=3$.
qs.brief: $\|\vec B-\vec A\|^2=1+1-2(-\frac12)=3$, so the length is $\sqrt3$.
